etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ernen, from Old English earnian, from Proto-West Germanic *aʀanōn, from Proto-Germanic *azanōną. This verb is denominal from the noun *azaniz (“harvest”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To gain (success, reward, recognition) through applied effort or work.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter II, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Carried somehow, somewhither, for some reason, on these surging floods, were these travelers, of errand not wholly obvious to their fellows, yet of such sort as to call into query alike the nature of their errand and their own relations. It is easily earned repetition to state that Josephine St. Auban's was a presence not to be concealed.

quote.citation: 2011 November 12, “International friendly: England 1-0 Spain”, in BBC Sport:
quote.text: England will not be catapulted among the favourites for Euro 2012 as a result of this win, but no victory against Spain is earned easily and it is right they take great heart from their efforts as they now prepare to play Sweden at Wembley on Tuesday.

You can have the s'mores: clearing the walkway of snow so well.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To receive payment for work or for a role or position held (regardless of whether effort was applied or whether the remuneration is deserved or commensurate).

quote.citation: 2015, Jason Zweig, The Devil's Financial Dictionary, PublicAffairs, →ISBN, page 1:
quote.text: After stuffing themselves and their clients full of dodgy mortgages at bogus prices with shoddy assertions of safety, many of the world's biggest banks toppled when housing prices fell. Meanwhile, financial executives whose irresponsible policies and slipshod oversight contributed to the collapse nevertheless earned—and kept—billions of dollars in bonuses, stock options, and other forms of incentive compensation. Many of them are still basking in baronial splendor, apparently unscathed even by the pangs of guilty conscience.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cause (someone) to receive payment or reward.

quote.citation: 1965, James Holledge, What Makes a Call Girl?, London: Horwitz Publications, page 99:
quote.text: '[T]hough I earned her a lot of money, I have nothing but regrets for what I did.'

definitions.definition: (transitive) To achieve by being worthy of.
(transitive, archaic) To curdle (milk), especially in the cheesemaking process.
(intransitive, obsolete) Of milk: to curdle, espcially in the cheesemaking process.
(transitive, obsolete) To strongly long or yearn (for something or to do something).[5]

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 3:
quote.text: And ever as he rode, his hart did earne / To prove his puissance in battell brave.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii], page 75, column 2:
quote.text: [M]y manly heart doth erne.  […]  Boy, briſsle thy Courage vp: For Falſtaffe hee is dead, and wee muſt erne therefore.

quote.citation: 1805, Walter Scott, “(please specify the page)”, in The Lay of the Last Minstrel: A Poem, London:  […]  [James Ballantyne] for Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, […], and A[rchibald] Constable and Co., […], →OCLC:
quote.text: They gleamed on many a dusky tarn , Haunted by the lonely earn
